opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real gap right now between the excitement and where the technology actually is. If you watch the demos online, you'd think general-purpose robots are going to be in every home next year. I understand why people feel that way, because the progress in the last two or three years has honestly been remarkable. Things like large models, vision-language-action models, and much better simulation-to-real transfer have changed what we thought was possible. Tasks that used to take a whole PhD thesis to get working on one robot, we can now do much more generally.

But from the inside, I'd say we should be careful. A demo is not a product. A demo shows that something can work once, maybe in a controlled environment, maybe after many tries. Real-world deployment means it has to work reliably, thousands of times, in messy and unstructured environments, around people, safely, and at a cost that makes sense. Going from 90% success to 99.9% success is often much harder than going from zero to 90%. That last stretch is where most of the time goes.

There's also a data problem that's unique to robotics. Language models could learn from the whole internet, but there's no internet-scale dataset of robots physically interacting with the world. We're still figuring out how to collect that data efficiently, whether through teleoperation, simulation, human videos, or some combination. Until that's solved, progress will be steady but not as explosive as in language.

So my view is cautiously optimistic. I think in the next few years we'll see robots doing useful work in more structured settings, like factories, warehouses, and logistics, where the environment is more predictable. General-purpose robots in the home that can do any chore you ask, I think that's further out, maybe closer to a decade. Expectations matter, because if the hype gets too far ahead of reality, there's a risk of disappointment and a funding winter. But I'm very confident the direction is right. It's a question of when, not if.

r001.rationale: The candidate says online demos make viewers think general-purpose robots will soon be in every home, then explains demos may work only once, in controlled settings, or after many tries.

r002.rationale: It describes remarkable recent progress but says reliable, safe, cost-effective deployment remains difficult, with broad home use perhaps a decade away.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the expectations are, frankly, ahead of where the technology is, but not in a way that worries me too much, because that gap is a very normal part of how these waves play out.

Let me explain what I mean. Over the past two or three years, people watched what happened with large language models, and the natural instinct was to say, okay, robotics is next, we just apply the same recipe and in two years we'll have a general-purpose robot in the home. And there are reasons to be optimistic. The foundation model approach really has changed robotics. We can now train a single policy across many tasks, many embodiments, and get transfer in a way that was basically impossible when I started in this field. The demos you see are real. The learning is real.

But there are some things that make robots different from language, and these are the parts that get underestimated. First, data. Language models trained on the entire internet. There is no internet of robot actions. Every bit of data we have, we have to collect, either through teleoperation, through simulation, or through the robot acting in the world. That's expensive and slow, and it's the main bottleneck. Second, the physical world punishes mistakes. If a chatbot gives you a slightly wrong answer, you shrug. If a robot drops a glass or bumps into a child, that's a very different failure. So the reliability bar is not ninety percent, it's closer to ninety-nine point something, and the last few percent in robotics is historically where most of the time goes. And third, hardware. Hands are still hard. Dexterity, tactile sensing, durability, cost, these things improve on a hardware timeline, not a software timeline.

So how do I actually assess the timelines? I think in terms of a sequence rather than a single moment. In structured environments, warehouses, factories, logistics, I think we're already there or very close. Those settings are constrained enough that today's methods work and you'll see real deployments scaling in the next couple of years. Semi-structured environments, like retail, hospitals, maybe commercial kitchens, I'd put that in the mid-term, several years. And the thing everyone imagines, a general-purpose humanoid folding your laundry and cooking dinner in an unfamiliar home, I think that is a longer road than the current excitement suggests. Not impossible, and I believe it will happen, but we should be honest that it requires solving problems we haven't solved yet.

What I'd say to people, especially investors and the public, is to separate two questions. One is, is the field moving fast? Yes, faster than I have ever seen. The other is, will the fully general product arrive on the timeline people are hoping for? Probably later than the most aggressive predictions. Both can be true at the same time. The danger is that if expectations are too inflated, we get a disappointment cycle, and robotics has been through those before. I'd much rather we celebrate the real progress, deploy where it works today, and let the harder problems take the time they need.

r001.rationale: The response attributes inflated expectations to applying the LLM trajectory to robotics, but does not say viewers mistake selectively showcased best-case robot demos for representative capability.

r002.rationale: It says progress is fast and general-purpose home robots remain a longer-term goal, but also says robotics is already deployed or close to deployment in structured settings. It does not characterize robotics broadly as far from practical deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between robots doing something impressive in a demo and robots being ready for everyday use. A demo shows that a task is possible. Real-world deployment requires the robot to do it reliably, repeatedly, and at a reasonable cost—even when the environment changes or something goes wrong.

So I’m optimistic about the progress, but cautious about timelines. We’ll probably see useful robots in more constrained settings first, where the task and environment are well defined. A general-purpose robot that can walk into any home and handle whatever you ask is a much higher bar. The question isn’t just, “When will robots be ready?” It’s, “Ready for which task, under what conditions, and with how much human assistance?”

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes demos from reliable everyday deployment, but does not say viewers mistake selectively showcased best-case demos for representative capability or that this inflates expectations.

r002.rationale: It expresses optimism about progress and caution about timelines, but does not state that progress is accelerating or that robotics remains far from practical deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between a robot doing something impressive in a demo and a robot being useful every day. In a demo, you can control the environment and choose the successful run. In the real world, the robot has to handle unexpected situations, work reliably, and be safe around people. And it has to do that at a cost that makes sense.

So I’m optimistic about the progress, but cautious about precise timelines. We’ll probably see robots become useful first in specific tasks and relatively structured environments. A general-purpose robot that can walk into any home and do whatever you ask is a much harder problem. The key question is less “When will robots be ready?” and more “Ready for which task, under what conditions, and with how much human help?”

r001.rationale: It contrasts controlled demos with real-world conditions, but does not say viewers mistake selectively showcased demos for representative capability or that this inflates readiness expectations.

r002.rationale: It expresses caution about timelines and says general-purpose home robots are harder, but does not state that progress still leaves robotics far from practical deployment.
